Part I
Getting Started
Chapter 1

Welcome to PAGEdesigner

PAGEdesigner is a desktop-publishing (DTP) program: a tool for arranging text, pictures, shapes and tables on a page exactly where you want them, and then printing the result or saving it as a PDF. It belongs to the just a… family of apps and works in the tradition of Serif's PagePlus — the same ideas, the same menus, in the same places.

What desktop publishing is

A word processor pours text down a page from top to bottom. A page-layout program is different: the page is a canvas, and everything on it — a headline, a column of body text, a photo, a price table, a logo — is a separate object you position freely. That freedom is what lets you make posters, flyers, newsletters, menus, business cards and booklets that look designed rather than typed.

If you have used Canva, Microsoft Publisher or Serif's PagePlus, you already know the idea. If you have only ever used a word processor, the single thing to unlearn is this: you no longer type down a page — you place things on it.

The object model

Everything you put on a page is an object, and there are only a handful of kinds:

  • Text frames — a box that holds a paragraph of body text, wrapping inside its edges;
  • Artistic text — a single line of display type you scale freely, for titles and mastheads;
  • Picture frames — a box that holds a photograph or image;
  • Shapes and lines — rectangles, ellipses, QuickShapes, rules and connectors;
  • Tables — a grid of cells for data;
  • Charts and QR codes — a picture generated from data you type.

Because they are all objects, the skills are shared: whatever the kind, you select it, move it, resize it, colour it, align it and layer it in exactly the same way. Learn those moves once (Chapter on Working with Objects) and they apply everywhere.

The just a… family

PAGEdesigner has a growing family of companions, built to work together:

  • WEBcreator makes websites the same way PAGEdesigner makes printed pages;
  • PAINTcanvas is the image editor — PAGEdesigner hands a photo to it for retouching and gets the result straight back;
  • DRAWmaster is for vector illustration and logos;
  • VIDEOeditor — a video editor in the spirit of Serif MoviePlus — is in the works.

They share the CREATORsuite launcher and a common Documents/just a… folder, so your work is always easy to find. Once you know one app, the others feel familiar.

About this guide

This User Guide is the complete reference. It is organised in parts: the first gets you working, the middle teaches each skill in depth with step-by-step procedures, then come worked projects you can follow start to finish, output and publishing, and finally a reference section — menus, shortcuts, a catalogue of every template, asset and shape, and a glossary.

NoteThroughout, a numbered “To …” box is a procedure you can follow exactly. A Tip suggests a faster or better way. A Remember box flags something easy to forget.

For a gentler first read, start with the Quick Start Guide (Help ▸ Quick Start), which takes you from a blank page to a finished newsletter in about a dozen short steps.

Conventions used here

A few conventions keep the instructions short:

  • Menu ▸ Command means “open this menu and choose this command”, e.g. File ▸ Export PDF….
  • Keys are shown like Ctrl+S; on a Mac read Ctrl as Cmd.
  • Click means the left mouse button; right-click opens a context menu; double-click opens whatever the object is for (a dialog, or edit-in-place for text).
  • Drag means press, move, release.
Chapter 2

Starting Out

This chapter covers the very first things: launching the program, the Startup Assistant that greets you, and the two ways to begin a document — from a ready-made design, or from a blank sheet of a chosen size.

Launching the program

Open just a… PAGEdesigner from the CREATORsuite launcher, from your system's application menu, or by running pagecreator in a terminal. The first time it opens it may take a moment to settle; after that it starts quickly.

The Startup Assistant

Each time it launches, PAGEdesigner shows the Startup Assistant — your hub for beginning work. Down its left side are its sections; the large area on the right shows what each offers.

To begin from the Startup Assistant

  1. Choose Start from a design to pick a ready-made template (see the next chapter), or
  2. New Publication to choose a blank paper size, or
  3. Open to reopen recent work or browse for a saved file.
  4. Click your choice to open a document and close the Assistant.
TipPrefer to start on a blank page every time? Untick Show this at startup at the bottom. You can always summon the Assistant again from File ▸ New.

Starting from a blank paper size

Choose New Publication to begin with an empty page at a standard size.

The presets are grouped so the right one is easy to find:

  • Documents — A4, A4 Landscape, A5, A3, US Letter, US Legal;
  • Business — business cards, letterhead, DL flyers, postcards, compliment slips;
  • Booklet & Folded — A5 and A4 booklets, greeting cards, tri-folds;
  • Large Format — A3, A2 and A1 posters.

To start a custom-sized document

  1. In New Publication, choose Custom size.
  2. Type a width and height (in millimetres) and a page count.
  3. Click Create. Your blank document opens at exactly that size.
NoteEvery thumbnail is drawn to the sheet’s true proportions, so a business card looks like a card and a poster like a poster — handy for choosing at a glance.

Opening and saving

PAGEdesigner documents are saved with a .pagc extension.

To save your work

  1. Choose File ▸ Save or press Ctrl+S.
  2. The first time, give the document a name. It is saved into your shared Documents/just a… folder by default, so the launcher can find it.
  3. Use File ▸ Save As… to keep a separate copy under a new name.

To open an existing document

  1. Choose File ▸ Open (Ctrl+O) and browse to a .pagc file, or
  2. pick a recent file from File ▸ Open Recent, or from the Open page of the Startup Assistant.

PAGEdesigner also opens files from the programs it stands in for: File ▸ Open PagePlus… reads a Serif PagePlus .ppp publication, and it can import a WebPlus site or a PDF, each as an editable document. Your original file is never altered.

Chapter 3

The Workspace

Everything you do happens in the workspace: your page in the middle, the tools down the left, the menus and toolbars along the top, and the panels on the right. This chapter names every part so the rest of the guide can refer to them.

A tour of the window

A new document opens with the page centred and everything you need arranged around it.

The parts are:

  • the menu bar and toolbars across the top;
  • the tool palette down the left edge;
  • the rulers framing the page;
  • the page itself in the centre, on its pasteboard;
  • the tabbed panels on the right;
  • the status bar along the bottom.

The tool palette

The vertical tool palette on the left holds the tools you draw and edit with.

From the top: the Pointer (select and move), the Pan and Zoom tools for getting around, then the object tools — Artistic text, Text frame, Picture, Table, Rectangle, Ellipse, Line and the QuickShapes. Lower down sit Rotate and Crop, and shortcuts to a bulleted list and the companion apps. Click a tool to select it; its name and a hint appear in the status bar.

TipPress Esc or click the Pointer at any time to stop drawing and go back to selecting.

Menus and toolbars

The menu bar gathers every command under File, Edit, View, Insert, Format, Arrange, the two Export items and Help. The complete menu reference is Appendix A.

Below the menus, the Standard toolbar carries the everyday buttons, and an Insert toolbar sits alongside it. Toolbars can be shown or hidden from View, and dragged to re-dock.

The panels

The tabbed panels on the right are where you inspect and fine-tune whatever is selected.

  • Pages — add, delete and reorder pages, and manage master pages;
  • Colour — set a fill, line or text colour with sliders or a hex value;
  • Swatches — a palette of saved colours, one click away;
  • Line — outline width, dashes and arrowheads;
  • Transparency — how much of what is behind an object shows through;
  • Transform — exact position, size and rotation;
  • Layers — stacking and grouping of objects.
TipAny panel can be shown or hidden from the View menu, and dragged out into its own floating window if you like more room.

Moving around and zooming

You will zoom in to place things precisely and out to judge the whole page.

To change the zoom

  1. Type or pick a level in the zoom box at the bottom-right, or
  2. hold Ctrl and scroll the mouse wheel, or
  3. choose View ▸ Zoom In / Zoom Out (Ctrl++ / Ctrl+−).

View ▸ Fit Page and Fit Width frame the whole page or its full width at once. The Pan tool — or holding the space bar and dragging — slides the page around when you are zoomed in.

Rulers, guides and the grid

The rulers along the top and left show position in your document's units. Drag out from a ruler to drop a guide line; objects snap to guides as you move them, which is how you keep columns, margins and rows of objects lined up.

To set up column and row guides

  1. Choose View ▸ Guides… to open the Guides & Columns dialog.
  2. Set the number of columns and their gutter (the gap between them), and rows if you want them.
  3. Tick Show guides and click OK. Non-printing guide lines divide the page for you to lay text and pictures against.

Turn snapping, the grid and the rulers themselves on or off from the View menu.

Part II
Core Skills
Chapter 4

Setting Up Pages

A publication is a stack of pages that share a size and, usually, a common background. This chapter covers adding and arranging pages, and the master pages that carry anything meant to repeat — a logo, a footer, a page number.

The Pages panel

Open the Pages panel to see every page in the document as a list.

To add, remove and reorder pages

  1. Click Add page beneath the list to insert a new page after the current one.
  2. Select a page and click Delete to remove it.
  3. Drag a page up or down the list, or use the move buttons, to change the running order.
  4. Double-click a page to go straight to it.
NoteA booklet (from the Booklet & Folded sizes) keeps its pages in printing order for you, so a folded A5 booklet imposes correctly when you print it.

Master pages

Anything that should appear on every page — a logo, a footer, a watermark, a page number — belongs on a master page. A master sits behind the ordinary pages that use it, so you draw the object once and it shows through everywhere.

To put a logo on every page

  1. In the Pages panel, choose New master page.
  2. On the master, place the logo (or footer, or whatever repeats) where you want it.
  3. Return to an ordinary page: the item now shows on it, and on every other page that uses this master.
  4. To change it later, choose Edit master page, adjust it once, and every page updates.
TipAlready built a page and only then realised several items repeat on others? Arrange ▸ Move Repeated Objects to Master Page… finds them and lifts them onto the master for you.

Page numbers

Automatic page numbers live on a master page, so every page shows its own number without any manual updating.

Add a small text frame to the master where the number should sit, then choose Insert ▸ Page Number. Each page that uses the master then prints its own number; insert or delete a page and the rest renumber themselves.

Document setup and margins

File ▸ Document Setup lets you revisit the page size, orientation and margins after you have started. Margins are guide lines, not hard limits — content can sit in the margin — but keeping body text inside them is what gives a page its comfortable, professional border of white space.

Chapter 5

Working with Objects

Text frames, pictures, shapes, tables and charts are all objects, and they are handled the same way. Master the moves in this chapter — select, move, size, rotate, align, order, group, lock — and they serve you everywhere in the program.

Selecting objects

To select objects

  1. Choose the Pointer tool.
  2. Click an object to select it — a frame of handles appears around it.
  3. Hold Shift and click more objects to add them to the selection.
  4. Or drag a box across empty space to select everything it touches.
  5. Press Esc (or click empty space) to deselect; Ctrl+A selects everything on the page.

Moving and resizing

With one or more objects selected:

  • Move — drag any selected object; the whole selection moves together.
  • Resize — drag a corner or edge handle. Dragging a corner keeps the proportions of a picture.
  • Nudge — tap the arrow keys to move a small, exact step at a time.
  • Rotate — drag the round handle above the object, or use the Rotate tool. Hold Shift to snap to 15° steps.
TipGuides and other objects give off a gentle snap as you drag past their edges and centres — let it do the aligning for you.

The Transform panel

When “close enough” is not enough, the Transform panel (and Arrange ▸ Transform…) lets you type exact numbers.

To place an object precisely

  1. Select the object.
  2. Open Transform and type its X and Y position, its width and height, or a rotation angle.
  3. Press Enter. This is the reliable way to make two objects exactly the same size, or to sit something a precise distance from the edge.

Aligning and distributing

Alignment is what turns a rough arrangement into a crisp one. Select two or more objects, then use Arrange ▸ Align:

  • Left / Centre / Right lines up their vertical edges or centres;
  • Top / Middle / Bottom lines up their horizontal edges or centres;
  • Centre on Page centres the selection on the sheet;
  • Distribute spaces three or more objects evenly.

A row of buttons, a grid of photos, a stack of headings — all look intentional once aligned.

Order, grouping and locking

Objects stack in the order you create them, newest on top. Use Arrange to change that:

  • Bring to Front / Send to Back, and Forward / Back One, so a caption can sit over a photo;
  • Group ties several objects together so they move and resize as one — ungroup to edit a part;
  • Lock / Unlock (Ctrl+L) pins something so you cannot nudge it by accident.
RememberLocked objects cannot be selected by dragging a box — that is the point. Unlock from Arrange ▸ Lock / Unlock when you need to move one again.

Cut, copy, paste and duplicate

The usual editing commands all apply to objects:

  • Ctrl+X / Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V cut, copy and paste;
  • Duplicate (Ctrl+D) drops a copy a little offset from the original;
  • Ctrl+Z undoes, Ctrl+Shift+Z redoes — there is a deep undo history, so experiment freely.
TipCopying an object and pasting it onto another page is the simplest way to reuse something you have built — a styled heading, a logo lock-up, a coloured panel.
Chapter 6

Text

Text is the heart of most publications. PAGEdesigner handles it the PagePlus way: body copy lives in frames you can link and flow, headlines are artistic text you scale freely, and styles keep a long document consistent.

Frame text

To add a block of body text

  1. Choose the Text frame tool.
  2. Drag a rectangle on the page — that is a text frame.
  3. Type, or paste; the text wraps inside the frame’s edges automatically.
  4. Switch to the Pointer to move or resize the frame; the text re-wraps to fit.

Flowing text between frames

When a frame holds more text than it can show, a red overflow marker appears in its corner. You can make the text continue in another frame — exactly how a newspaper runs a story across columns and pages.

To flow a long story across two frames

  1. Draw a second text frame where the story should continue.
  2. Click the overflow marker on the first frame, then click the second frame.
  3. The overflowing text flows into the second frame. Resize or delete either frame and the text re-flows through the chain automatically.

Artistic text

Where frame text is for paragraphs, artistic text is a single line you can scale to any size — the tool for mastheads, titles and pull-quotes. Choose the Artistic text tool, click, and type; then drag a corner handle to make it as large as you like. Because it is vector, it stays razor-sharp at any size, unlike a picture of type.

Fonts, size, colour and alignment

Select some text — a word, a line or a whole frame — and set its look from the Format menu and the text controls:

  • Font and size;
  • Bold (Ctrl+B), Italic (Ctrl+I) and Underline (Ctrl+U);
  • Colour, from the Colour panel;
  • Alignment — left, centred, right or justified;
  • Line spacing, to open a dense block up or draw a loose one in.
TipFor running text, left-aligned is easiest to read; reserve centred text for short headings and justified text for narrow columns where you want a clean right edge.

Drop caps and lists

Two classic touches live in the Format menu:

To start a paragraph with a drop cap

  1. Click in the paragraph.
  2. Choose Format ▸ Drop Cap. The first letter enlarges and sets into the lines below — the traditional way to open an article.

To turn paragraphs into a bulleted or numbered list

  1. Select the paragraphs.
  2. Choose a style from Format ▸ Lists / Bullets — a disc, circle or square bullet, or 1-2-3, a-b-c or i-ii-iii numbering.
  3. The list indents neatly; a numbered list renumbers itself if you add or remove an item.

The Fonts panel and special fonts

PAGEdesigner ships with a set of distinctive display, script and slab fonts — the kind you reach for on a poster title, a certificate or a café menu — the same open-licence faces the old Serif packages bundled. They are installed with the app, so they are there even on a computer that has never seen them, and they appear in every font list.

The quickest way to choose one is the Fonts panel in the studio (the tab beside Layers). It shows each font as a large sample so you can see it before you commit:

To apply a special font

  1. Select a text frame or artistic text (or highlight some words while editing).
  2. Open the Fonts panel and click a sample.
  3. The text takes on that font at once. The same fonts are also in the ordinary font drop-down, listed by name.
TipPair a decorative font for the headline with a plain one (such as Open Sans) for the body — one personality per page is plenty.

Text styles

When a document has several headings, you want them to match without setting each by hand. Text styles do that: apply a named style — Heading, Subheading, Body — from Format ▸ Text Styles, and every piece of text with that style looks the same. Restyle the document later by changing the style once, and everything using it updates. Styles are what keep a long, multi-page document consistent and quick to re-skin.

Find &amp; Replace

In a long document, changing a word everywhere by hand is slow and easy to get wrong — miss one, and the inconsistency shows. Find & Replace does it in one pass, searching the text on every page (and the master pages) at once.

To change a word or phrase throughout the document

  1. Choose Edit ▸ Find & Replace… or press Ctrl+H.
  2. Type the text to look for in Find what, and its replacement in Replace with.
  3. Tick Match case if the capitals matter (so Rose the name is not caught by rose the flower).
  4. Click Replace to change the first match, or Replace All to change every one. PAGEdesigner reports how many it changed.
NoteReplacement is tag-safe: it only ever changes the words you see, never the hidden formatting around them, so bold, colour and links survive untouched. And it is a single undo — one Ctrl+Z puts every change back.

Table of Contents

A multi-page document — a booklet, a report, a programme — deserves a contents page. PAGEdesigner builds one from your page list, so you never have to type titles and page numbers by hand or keep them in step as the document grows.

To insert a table of contents

  1. Go to the page where the contents should appear.
  2. Choose Insert ▸ Table of Contents….
  3. Give it a heading (Contents by default) and choose whether to leave out the page it sits on.
  4. Click OK. A text frame drops in, listing every page with its page number, each line linked to its page.

Once inserted it is an ordinary text frame: restyle it, change the type, move it — whatever you would do to any text. When you later add, rename or reorder pages, rebuild it in one step:

To update the contents after changing pages

  1. Choose Insert ▸ Update Table of Contents.
  2. Every contents frame in the document is regenerated from the current page list, with the right titles and numbers.
NoteThe page numbers follow the same counting as a Page Number Field — a page’s position in the document — so the contents and the running page numbers always agree.

Wrapping text, and spell check

Text can wrap around a picture or shape, so words flow around the artwork rather than disappearing behind it — give the object a wrap setting and place it over the text column.

To check spelling before you print

  1. Choose Format ▸ Check Spelling… or press F7.
  2. Step through each flagged word; choose a suggestion, ignore it, or add it to the dictionary.
Chapter 7

Pictures

Pictures bring a page to life. PAGEdesigner keeps them in frames you can crop and style, and hands off to PAINTcanvas when a photo needs real editing.

Picture frames

To place a photograph

  1. Choose the Picture tool and drag a box — a picture frame, shown as a grey placeholder.
  2. Double-click the frame and choose an image file.
  3. The picture fits the frame. Design the layout first with empty frames, and drop the photos in later — a frame can wait.
NoteKeeping images in frames (rather than loose on the page) is what lets you resize the hole and the picture independently, and swap one photo for another without disturbing the layout.

Fitting, cropping and borders

A picture either fills its frame (cropping to the edges) or sits inside it. To show only part of a photo, use the Crop tool:

To crop a picture

  1. Select the picture and choose the Crop tool.
  2. Drag the handles inward to hide the parts you do not want.
  3. Switch back to the Pointer. The hidden area is kept, so you can re-crop later.

Round the frame's corners or give it an outline from the Line panel to finish it off.

Editing a photo in PAINTcanvas

When a photo needs more than cropping — brightening, retouching, removing a background — PAGEdesigner sends it to its sister app.

To edit a picture in PAINTcanvas

  1. Select the picture.
  2. Click Edit in PAINTcanvas on the Apps toolbar.
  3. Make your edits in PAINTcanvas and save. The edited version comes straight back into your page, in place.
TipNo photo to hand? Create an image with AI can generate one from a short description, dropped straight into the selected frame.
Chapter 8

Shapes, Lines and QuickShapes

Shapes and lines give a page structure and emphasis — a coloured band for a masthead, a rule between stories, a star on an offer. PAGEdesigner's QuickShapes give you two dozen ready outlines, each with a fill, an outline and optional effects.

Drawing shapes and lines

To draw a shape or a line

  1. Choose the Rectangle, Ellipse or Line tool (or a QuickShape).
  2. Drag on the page to draw it. Hold Shift to constrain a perfect square, circle, or a straight / 45° line.
  3. Switch to the Pointer to move, resize or recolour it.

A thin filled rectangle makes a neat rule between stories — the green bars in the sample newsletter are exactly that.

The QuickShape catalogue

QuickShapes are ready-made outlines. Pick one from the tool palette or from Insert ▸ QuickShapes, drag it out, then resize and recolour it like any other shape.

They cover geometry (triangles, diamonds, polygons), stars and bursts, arrows and a chevron, and the expressive shapes — heart, lightning bolt, speech bubble, cloud — plus banner shapes (ribbon, pennant, seal) ready for a badge or a title bar.

Fills, outlines, dashes and arrowheads

Every shape has a fill and an outline, set from the Colour and Line panels. A line can be made dashed and finished with arrowheads at either or both ends — a dashed line with an arrowhead is the simplest callout you can draw. Set the outline width in the Line panel; set it to zero for a shape with no border at all.

Drop shadow and glow

Filter effects lift an object off the page.

To add a drop shadow or a glow

  1. Select the shape (or picture, or text).
  2. Open the Effects dialog.
  3. Tick drop shadow and set its colour, blur, offset and strength — or tick outer glow for a soft halo.
  4. Click OK.

A drop shadow adds depth behind a panel; an outer glow draws the eye to a price or a highlight.

Chapter 9

Colour, Fills and Transparency

Colour ties a publication together. PAGEdesigner offers solid colours, swatches you keep to hand, smooth gradient fills, coordinated colour schemes, and adjustable transparency.

Applying colour

To colour an object

  1. Select it.
  2. Open the Colour panel and choose the Fill, Line or Text tab, to say which part you are colouring.
  3. Pick a colour with the sliders, or type a hex value like #2a7d6b.

Swatches and colour schemes

The Swatches panel keeps a palette of colours one click away, so a document stays consistent — save a colour you use often and reuse it everywhere rather than matching hex values by hand.

A colour scheme goes further: it is a small set of coordinated colours applied across the whole publication at once. Pick a different scheme and every object that uses it recolours together, so you can try a document warm, then cool, then monochrome, in seconds.

Gradient fills

A gradient fades one colour smoothly into another across a shape — a sky behind a headline, a soft panel behind text.

To fill a shape with a gradient

  1. Select the shape.
  2. Open the Gradient Fill dialog.
  3. Choose a start and end colour, and for a linear gradient, an angle.
  4. Click OK. The gradient scales with the object as you resize it.

Picture and texture fills

A shape need not be filled with a flat colour or a gradient — it can be filled with a picture. Drop a photo into a heading banner, a paper texture behind a certificate, a pattern inside a star.

To fill a shape with a picture

  1. Select the shape (or a text box or button).
  2. Choose Format ▸ Picture Fill… and pick an image file.
  3. Choose how it should fit — Stretch to fill the shape, or Tile it (repeat the picture).
  4. Click OK. The outline, corners and any shadow or glow still apply over the top.
TipTo go back to a plain colour, choose Format ▸ Remove Picture Fill.

Replacing a colour everywhere

Change your mind about a colour after building a whole publication? You do not have to re-select every object. Replace Colour swaps one colour for another across every page at once — fills, outlines, text, gradients, tables and charts included.

To replace a colour across the whole publication

  1. Choose Format ▸ Replace Colour….
  2. From the list of colours actually used in the document, click the one you want to change (each shows how many times it is used).
  3. Pick the colour to change it to.
  4. Click Replace. Every instance updates at once — and Undo (Ctrl+Z) reverts it if you change your mind.
NoteThis is the quick way to re-brand a finished document, or to fix a colour that prints differently from how it looked on screen.

Transparency

Transparency lets what is behind an object show through it. A half-transparent coloured rectangle laid over a photo makes a tint you can read white text on; a faint shape becomes a watermark. Set an object's transparency from the Transparency panel — from fully solid to barely there.

Chapter 10

Tables, Charts, QR Codes and More

Beyond free text, PAGEdesigner builds the structured pieces a real publication needs: tables for data, charts that picture it, scannable QR codes, a calendar wizard and a mail merge for personalised runs.

Tables

To insert a table

  1. Choose Insert ▸ Table (or the Table tool).
  2. Set the number of rows and columns.
  3. Type straight into the cells; press Tab to move to the next cell.
  4. Give the header row its own fill, and drag the borders to size the table or individual columns.

A table is ideal for a price list, a timetable, or the “Dates for the diary” box in the sample newsletter.

Charts

To insert a chart

  1. Choose Insert ▸ Chart….
  2. Pick a type — bar, line or pie.
  3. Type the data, one “label, value” per line, and give the chart a title.
  4. Click OK. Double-click the chart any time to change its data or type.

QR codes

To add a QR code

  1. Choose Insert ▸ QR Code….
  2. Type what it should link to — a web address, an email (mailto:…), a phone number (tel:…) or any text.
  3. Click OK, then resize it like a picture. It stays sharp, so a phone camera reads it from a printed flyer or poster.

Calendars and mail merge

Insert ▸ Calendar… generates a monthly or yearly calendar you can drop onto a page and style — handy for a community newsletter or a printed planner.

Insert ▸ Mail Merge… takes a list of names and addresses from a CSV file and produces one copy of the document per row, filling placeholder fields with each person's details — for letters, labels or personalised flyers.

Part III
Templates, Assets & Design
Chapter 11

The Template Library

PAGEdesigner ships with 18 ready-made design templates — posters, flyers, newsletters, menus, cards, a certificate and social-media posts. This chapter is an illustrated catalogue of every one; pick the nearest fit and make it yours.

Starting from a template

The fastest way to a finished document is to start from a design template — a complete layout you make your own. When PAGEdesigner opens, the Startup Assistant shows the gallery; click a template and it opens as an ordinary document, fully editable.

To build a document from a template

  1. In the Startup Assistant, choose Start from a design.
  2. Click a template that is close to what you want. It opens laid out.
  3. Replace the placeholder headings and body text with your own words.
  4. Double-click a picture frame to drop in your photo.
  5. Recolour, move or delete anything; then print or export a PDF.
RememberA template is just a normal document once it opens — there is nothing special or locked about it. Change everything freely.

Chapter 12

The Asset Library

The asset library holds 20 drop-in graphics — callouts, badges, banners, arrows and decorations — grouped by kind. This chapter illustrates every one.

What the asset library is

Where a template is a whole page, an asset is a single ready-made graphic you drop onto a page you are already building — the finishing touches that make a poster or flyer pop.

To add an asset to a page

  1. Choose Insert ▸ Asset….
  2. Browse the gallery and click one; it lands in the middle of the page, selected.
  3. Drag it where you want it, resize it, recolour it from the Colour panel, and — on a badge or banner — click the words and retype them.
TipA “SALE” badge becomes a “½ PRICE” badge in seconds, and a green ribbon becomes a red one with a single colour change — assets are built from the same editable shapes as everything else.

Chapter 13

Designing a Page

The tools are only half the job; the other half is using them well. This chapter distils the handful of principles that separate a page that looks designed from one that looks typed — the same instincts a Canva or a PagePlus user relies on.

Start with a grid

Before placing anything, set up column guides (View ▸ Guides…). Laying every object against the same few lines — even when the page looks busy — is the single biggest thing that makes a layout feel calm and intentional. Two or three columns suit most flyers and newsletters.

Alignment and white space

Line things up, and give them room. Nothing should sit a few stray pixels off from its neighbour — select and Align. And resist filling every corner: generous margins and space around a headline make a page look confident, not empty. Crowding is what reads as amateur.

A limited palette and two fonts

Pick two or three colours and stick to them — a colour scheme makes this effortless. Do the same with type: one font for headings, one for body, and vary size and weight rather than adding more fonts. Restraint looks professional; variety for its own sake looks noisy.

Hierarchy: lead the eye

Decide what the reader should see first, second, third — and make the sizes say so. A big headline, a clear subhead, calm body text. A poster has a loud first line and little else; a newsletter has a masthead, then story headings, then columns. If everything shouts, nothing is heard.

Contrast and emphasis

Use contrast deliberately: dark text on a light panel, one accent colour on an otherwise quiet page, a single badge or burst to mark the one thing that matters (the price, the date, the offer). A drop shadow or a filled band behind a headline is often all the emphasis a page needs.

Part IV
Worked Projects
Chapter 14

Project: A Community Newsletter

This project builds the one-page newsletter you have seen throughout the guide, from a blank A4 page to a finished layout — putting the skills of Part II to work in order.

Set up the page

To start the newsletter

  1. In the Startup Assistant choose New Publication ▸ A4.
  2. Open View ▸ Guides… and set two columns with a 5 mm gutter, so you have a frame to work against.

Draw a filled rectangle across the full width of the top of the page, with no outline, in your main colour. This band is the masthead's background.

Add the masthead

With the Artistic text tool, type the paper's name over the band and scale it large and white. Add a small frame of text beneath it for the issue line.

Place the lead story

To lay out the lead story

  1. Add an artistic text headline below the masthead.
  2. Draw a text frame in the left column and type (or paste) the story; it wraps to the column.
  3. Draw a picture frame in the right column and drop in a photo; add a small caption frame beneath it.

Add the diary table

Below the photo, add a second heading and an Insert ▸ Table grid for the list of dates. Give its header row the light tint from your scheme.

Finish and export

Rule a thin coloured line across the foot of the page and add a small footer frame. Run a spell check (F7), then File ▸ Export PDF….

TipSave this as your own template: next issue, open it, change the words and the photo, and you are done in minutes.
Chapter 15

Project: An Event Poster

A poster has one job: to be read across a room. This short project shows the poster way of thinking — one loud message, little else — using a large-format page.

A poster is mostly one thing

Start from New Publication at A3 or A2 (or the Event poster template as a head start). A poster is built around a single dominant element: the event name, huge, and the one fact the reader must take away — the date, or the price.

Build it

To lay out the poster

  1. Fill the page with a background — a bold colour, a gradient, or a full-bleed photo in a picture frame.
  2. Add the event name as artistic text, as large as it will go.
  3. Add a second line for the single key fact, and a smaller block for the details at the foot.
  4. Drop a badge asset (a burst or seal) on the one thing you want noticed.
  5. Add a QR code that links to tickets or more information.
RememberIf you find yourself shrinking the title to fit more words in, cut the words instead. A poster that tries to say everything says nothing.
Chapter 16

Project: Business Cards and Folded Cards

Small formats have their own discipline: every millimetre counts, and the piece will be cut and sometimes folded. This project covers a business card and a folded greeting card.

A business card

Start from a Business card size or template. The whole design is a name, a role, and two or three ways to reach you — balanced, aligned, and sitting clear of the edges.

To make a business card

  1. Choose the business-card page size.
  2. Keep all text a few millimetres inside the edge — a guillotine is never perfectly accurate.
  3. Use the Insert ▸ Contact detail items to pull your name, email and phone from Settings.
  4. Export a PDF; for a print shop, turn on bleed and crop marks in the export options.

A folded card

For a greeting card or thank-you card, start from a folded size. Remember that the panels print on one sheet and fold — the front is not the first thing in reading order.

NoteBooklet and folded sizes impose the pages in the right printing order for you, so you can design in reading order and trust the print to come out folded correctly.
Chapter 17

Project: A Certificate or Voucher

A certificate is a landscape page built around symmetry and a little ceremony — a good exercise in centring, borders and restrained ornament.

Build a certificate

To make a certificate

  1. Start from the Certificate template, or a landscape A4 page.
  2. Add a decorative border (a shape with a thick outline, or a banner asset at the top).
  3. Centre everything: title, “awarded to”, the name line, and the reason, using Align ▸ Centre on Page.
  4. Add a seal or star badge asset, and lines for a signature and date.
TipA voucher is the same idea at a smaller size, with a value and an expiry date — and a QR code the till can scan.
Part V
Output & Publishing
Chapter 18

Checking Your Work

A few minutes checking before you publish saves a reprint later. PAGEdesigner gives you a spell check and a preflight look-over.

Spell check and proofreading

Run Format ▸ Check Spelling… (F7) as a last pass. Then read the page itself: a spell checker cannot tell you that a headline is missing a word, or that a date is wrong. Read every heading and every number aloud.

Preflight

File ▸ Preflight looks over the document for the common problems — an overflowing text frame, an object hanging off the page edge, a very low-resolution picture — and lists anything worth a second look before you commit it to paper or PDF.

Chapter 19

Printing and Exporting

When the layout is ready, you put it into the world — on paper, as a PDF, or as an eBook. This chapter covers each, and importing work from other programs.

Previewing before you print

Before committing a document to paper or PDF, look it over whole. File ▸ Print / PDF Preview shows every page exactly as it will come out, one after another, so you can catch a stray object or a page in the wrong order.

From the preview you can go straight to Print… or Export PDF…, or close it and keep editing.

Printing

To print the document

  1. Choose File ▸ Print.
  2. Pick the printer, the pages and the number of copies.
  3. Check the preview, then print.

Exporting a PDF

A PDF is the standard way to send a document to a print shop or share it online.

To export a PDF

  1. Choose File ▸ Export PDF… (Ctrl+E).
  2. Choose a file name and location.
  3. For professional printing, turn on bleed and crop marks so the printer can trim to the edge cleanly.
  4. Click Export.
NotePAGEdesigner’s PDF is vector: text and shapes stay razor-sharp at any size, and the file is small. It is the best format for anything that will be printed.

Imposition and booklet printing

Imposition is the printer's art of arranging several document pages onto one larger sheet, so that after printing, folding and trimming they end up in the right order. PAGEdesigner offers it both in the Export PDF dialog (the Layout drop-down) and from the Print / PDF Preview, which shows the composed sheets before you commit.

  • 1-up (normal) — one document page per sheet. This is the default, and what you want for ordinary printing or sending a PDF to a print shop.
  • 2-up — two pages side by side on each sheet: a quick way to proof, or to print a simple landscape leaflet.
  • 4-up — four pages (two across, two down) on each sheet, for thumbnails, labels or small cards.
  • Booklet — pages reordered into saddle-stitch folding sequence: print double-sided, fold the stack in half and staple the spine, and the pages read 1, 2, 3… in order. PAGEdesigner pads the count to a multiple of four with blank pages, as the fold requires.

To print a folded booklet

  1. Choose File ▸ Print / PDF Preview and set Layout to Booklet to see the imposed sheets.
  2. Choose Export PDF… (or Print…) from the preview, keeping the Booklet layout.
  3. Print the PDF double-sided (flip on the short edge), fold the stack in half, and staple along the fold.
RememberFor a booklet, your document should read in simple page order (1, 2, 3…). PAGEdesigner does the folding arithmetic; you supply the pages in reading order.

Exporting an eBook

File ▸ Export eBook… writes a reflowable EPUB from the text on your pages — each page becomes a chapter, with a contents list, ready to read on a phone, tablet or e-reader. Where a PDF preserves your exact layout, an eBook lets the reader's device choose the type size and re-flow the words to fit its screen — right for a long, text-led document, less so for a poster.

Importing from PagePlus, WebPlus and PDF

PAGEdesigner opens work from the programs it stands in for. File ▸ Open PagePlus… reads a Serif PagePlus .ppp publication; it can import a WebPlus site, and place a PDF as an editable document. In each case your original file is left untouched, so there is no risk in trying.

Chapter 23

Appendix D — Glossary

The desktop-publishing words used in this guide.

A–Z

Artistic text
A single line of display type you scale freely; vector, so always sharp.
Bleed
Extra colour or image past the trim edge, so a cut leaves no white sliver.
Crop marks
Corner ticks on a PDF that show a print shop where to trim.
Drop cap
An enlarged first letter set into the opening lines of a paragraph.
Flow
Running text on from one frame to the next, newspaper-style.
Frame
A box that holds text or a picture; you size the box and its contents independently.
Gradient
A smooth fade from one colour to another across a shape.
Gutter
The gap between two columns.
Master page
A page behind the others whose content repeats on every page that uses it.
Object
Anything you place on a page — text, picture, shape, table, chart.
Preflight
An automatic check for common problems before output.
QuickShape
A ready-made shape outline (star, arrow, speech bubble…).
Swatch
A saved colour kept one click away.
Vector
Artwork defined by maths, not pixels — sharp at any size.
Chapter 24

Appendix E — Troubleshooting

Quick answers to common snags.

Common questions

A red mark shows in the corner of a text frame.
The frame holds more text than it can show. Make the frame bigger, shrink the text, or flow it into a second frame.
My picture looks fuzzy in the PDF.
The image file is too low-resolution for the size you have printed it. Use a larger original, or make the frame smaller.
Text or colour is being cut off at the page edge when printed.
Keep content a few millimetres inside the edge, and turn on bleed in the PDF export if a design is meant to run to the edge.
I can't select an object.
It may be locked (Arrange ▸ Lock / Unlock) or on a master page (edit the master), or behind another object (use the Layers panel).
Everything I type goes into one line and won't wrap.
You are using Artistic text, which is a single line. Use a Text frame for anything more than a title.
The app won't start on Linux Mint.
Run the installer again from a terminal; it sets up its own private Python environment automatically if the system one is missing.
